How a Sporting™ layout and round work

Sporting™ In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ the shooting ground is divided into layouts. A layout is a group of shooting stands that together make up one round of 25 targets: 15 singles and 5 doubles.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 2 · What a layout must offer

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Layouts are built in one of two ways. In the older type, 3 stands share 5 traps. The newer type is called a line. A line of 4 stands has three stands with 4 traps and one stand (no. 2 or 3) with 3 traps. A line of 5 stands has 3 traps at each stand. A line of 3 stands with 5 traps each is allowed only for a Grand Prix.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 2 · Number of traps and targets per layout type

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

A shooting stand is where the shooter stands: a 1 m square or a circle 1 m across. It should be level where possible, and at least not slippery (a safety rule). The rest of the squad (the group of shooters who shoot together) waits nearby, close enough to follow but without distracting the shooter.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 2 · Size and surface of the shooting stand

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Traps are placed to suit the terrain, often partly hidden by bushes or trees. The targets copy real game: flying across, towards you, away from you or at an angle (quartering), high or low, in the open or through trees. The traps of a stand are lettered from left to right as seen from the stand: A, B, C and so on (the rulebook names A to D). The menu and the score sheet use these letters.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 2 · Trap types and letters

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

In front of each stand there is a target menu. It lists the traps in shooting order and names any special targets: 90 mm, 70 mm or 60 mm, battue or rabbit. Before the competition the referees check that the traps match the menu. Shooters read it before stepping onto the stand; see Reading the target menu.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 2 · Target menu at the stand

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Each trajectory has a difficulty class: class A is broken by an average shooter more than 80% of the time, class B 60–80%, class C 40–60%. For a stand the rules recommend one A, two B and one C trajectory. So a class C target is meant to be hard, and a miss there is no disaster.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 2 · Difficulty classes A, B and C

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

A Sporting™ competition is counted in rounds of 25 targets. An international event is 200 targets, so eight rounds; each round is shot on one layout (a set of shooting stands) or one line.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 16 · 200 targets in rounds of 25

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Shooters go round in squads of up to six; who goes in which squad is decided by a draw. At each stand everyone shoots the singles first, then the doubles. Who shoots first changes from stand to stand, and changes again when the doubles begin. The others wait close by without distracting the person shooting.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 16 · Squads of six and rotation

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Tip: When your name is called, be ready at once, with cartridges and kit for the whole round. Step onto the stand only when it is your turn and the shooter before you has left it.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 8 · Be ready; wait for the stand to clear

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

The referee, or a person the referee supervises, keeps the scorecard, marking each target under its trap letter. When leaving a stand, each shooter checks the score; if you disagree, tell the referee straight away, and the referee's decision is final.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 16 · Recording results and checking your score

Tip: Compak® Sporting is laid out differently: five stations on one small field, and the squad moves along the line. See How a Compak® Sporting layout works.

Key points

  • One layout gives one round of 25 targets: 15 singles and 5 doubles. An international event is 200 targets.
  • Traps are lettered A, B, C… from left to right as seen from the stand; the menu gives the order and special targets.
  • Difficulty classes: class A is broken by an average shooter more than 80% of the time, class B 60–80%, class C 40–60%.
  • Squads of up to six; singles first, then doubles; the order rotates.
  • Check your score when leaving each stand; the referee decides.
Stand Talk

  • Coach Layout three is the hard one today — lots of minis in the trees.

    Meaning: On the third layout there are many small targets flying through trees.

  • Coach On this stand, read the menu before you step in.

    Meaning: Check the order of traps and special targets first.

  • Coach Stand two is a class C target, don't worry about it.

    Meaning: The target is graded as hard; a miss is expected.

  • Referee Singles first, then doubles.

    Meaning: The standard order at every stand.

  • Referee Read the menu: the traps go A, B, C.

    Meaning: The menu board lists the traps in the order they will be shot.

  • Referee Next shooter.

    Meaning: The referee calls the next person onto the stand.

  • Referee Check your score before you leave the stand.

    Meaning: Any disagreement must be raised now, not later.

For the interpreter
  • In some languages the everyday word for “stand” means the whole sport or the shooting ground. Choose one word for the shooter's 1 m place and keep it all session.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. How many targets does one Sporting™ layout give, and how are they split?

    1. 20: 10 singles and 5 doubles
    2. 25: all singles
    3. 25: 15 singles and 5 doubles
    4. 50: 25 singles and 25 doubles
    Answer

    25: 15 singles and 5 doubles

    Each layout type gives 15 singles plus 5 doubles, which is 25 targets.

  2. In what order does a squad shoot at a stand?

    1. Doubles first, then singles, in a fixed order
    2. Singles first, then doubles, in rotation
    3. Each shooter shoots the whole stand in one go
    4. The shooters agree on the order themselves
    Answer

    Singles first, then doubles, in rotation

    Singles come first, then doubles, in rotation, unless the jury decides otherwise.

  3. Leaving the stand, a shooter sees that a hit was marked as a miss. What should he do?

    1. Wait for the end of the round and appeal to the jury
    2. Correct the card himself
    3. Ask the squad to vote
    4. Tell the referee at once; the referee decides
    Answer

    Tell the referee at once; the referee decides

    Scores are checked when leaving each stand; the referee alone decides, and there is no appeal afterwards.
